title: How the 1997–98 El Niño developed
description: Evidence-based reconstruction of the 1997–98 El Niño (in progress): preconditions, westerly wind events, the MJO, the Indian Ocean and termination, with timeline, evidence table and verified references.
lit_cutoff: open, updated as new studies appear
status_note: Stages 1–3 of 5 (23 Oct 2026): 93 Crossref queries; the 72 references cited are each matched to their Crossref record (one, Bergman et al. 2001, read in full from a private copy) and every available abstract was read; monthly data Jul 1995 – Dec 1998 assembled; timeline (22 rows) and evidence table (17 factors) drafted from abstracts, one full text (Bergman et al. 2001) and CPC/PMEL data. In progress: reanalysis MJO and westerly-burst diagnostics, TAO moorings and island sea level (running in GitHub Actions); full texts requested. Not yet written: the prose sections (stage 4) and verification (stage 5).

sections.title: Evidence base: scope, index and data
sections.html:
Primary index: NOAA's Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), official since 1 February 2026 [1] [2]. On RONI the 1997–98 peak is +2.28 (NDJ 1997); on the traditional ONI it is +2.37. The two agree within 0.1 °C for this event, unlike 1982–83 (RONI +2.40, ONI +2.14).

Observing system in 1997. The first strong El Niño observed from start to finish by the TOGA observing system — the TAO array of moored buoys, drifting buoys, island tide gauges, ship XBT lines — and by satellite winds, SST and TOPEX/Poseidon sea level (from 1992) [3] [12] [16] [17]. Onset, growth and termination are therefore documented daily along the equator, which allows heat-budget and wave analyses that were impossible for 1982. Argo did not yet exist; the subsurface off the equator and outside the array remains less certain.

table.note: RONI and ONI are three-month means centred on the month. SOI and trade-wind indices are standardized (negative = El Niño-like). OLR in W m⁻² (negative = more convection). Heat content in °C vs 1981–2010; WWV in 10¹⁴ m³; DMI in °C; PDO standardized.

timeline: La Niña: RONI from −0.41 (JAS 1995) to a minimum of −1.02 (OND 1995); back to −0.58 by FMA 1996.
Strong trades pile warm water in the west.
Warm water volume turns positive in December 1995 (+0.05 × 10¹⁴ m³) and stays positive all of 1996 (+0.26 to +0.85); heat content east of the Date Line near zero (−0.47 to +0.17 °C).
Recharge of the equatorial warm-water reservoir after La Niña, the precondition in recharge-oscillator theory.
ENSO-neutral, slightly cool: RONI −0.20 to −0.37; Niño 1+2 −0.7 to −1.6 °C (OISST).
Warm western-Pacific SST and an eastward-extended warm pool; the same autumn pattern preceded 1989–90 (aborted event) and 1981–82.
A warm, eastward-extended pool favours MJO convection over the western Pacific.
Equatorial cold SST and high SLP in the east; off-equatorial warm SST and anomalous cyclones in the far west; equatorial wind anomalies over the western Pacific switch from easterly to westerly.
First strong westerly wind event of the onset series; two exceptionally strong MJOs during winter 1996–97 (Dec 1996 and Feb 1997) cool the western Pacific through cloud shading and then evaporation.
MJO-embedded westerly bursts begin forcing downwelling Kelvin waves; surface-flux cooling in the west.
Westerly bursts embedded in the active MJO are greatly enhanced in the western Pacific by equatorial twin cyclones, induced by northerly cold surges from East Asia and the western North Pacific.
Extratropical cold surges → twin cyclones → amplified bursts.
First warming near the Date Line; heat content rises to +0.56 °C (Jan) and +1.00 °C (Feb); warm water volume +1.64 and +2.14 × 10¹⁴ m³.
Kelvin-wave deepening of the thermocline on top of the recharged state.

The strongest westerly wind event of the series. Model response: far-western cooling of about 0.8 °C, the eastern edge of the warm pool displaced about 2000 km in a month, warming of about 0.5 °C along the Kelvin-wave path; nonlinear surface jets near 1 m s⁻¹ at the warm-pool edge. Western-Pacific 850 hPa trade index −3.1 (standardized) for the month.
Kelvin wave plus rapid eastward advection of the warm pool's edge; the atmospheric response to these SST changes favours further westerlies.
High (event observations + ocean and atmosphere model experiments)

Warming appears in the far eastern Pacific (Niño 1+2 −0.45 °C in Feb, +0.23 °C in Mar, +0.80 °C in Apr); a slower westward-spreading warm anomaly from the coast later merges with the eastward-moving one.
Coastal arrival of the earlier Kelvin waves.

Central-Pacific SST warms as a downwelling Kelvin wave forced by the February MJO passes; the warming is mainly zonal temperature advection by strong eastward currents, and conditions do not revert afterwards.
Kelvin-wave-induced advection; a lasting change in winds, currents and SST gradient.
Another westerly wind event (one of the three, with Dec 1996 and Mar 1997, that differ most from 1996). Warm water volume peaks at +3.12 × 10¹⁴ m³; heat content +2.17 °C.
Recharged reservoir at its maximum as coupling begins.

In an ocean model, about 40% of the Niño 3 anomaly comes from the initial thermal state six months earlier and about 50% from wind stress, concentrated at the time and place of the Dec 1996, Mar 1997 and Apr 1997 westerly events; relative to 1996, wind stress is the main difference.
Quantitative split between precondition and wind triggers.
High for the model result; one model
Coupling established: RONI AMJ +0.83, MJJ +1.20; SOI −1.3 and −1.4; central-Pacific OLR −25.7 and −26.8 W m⁻²; Niño 1+2 +1.83 and +2.79 °C.
Bjerknes feedback takes over once the central and eastern warm regions join.
End of the westerly-burst series that ran from December 1996.
Rapid growth: RONI JJA +1.50 → SON +2.22; central-Pacific trade index −4.1 and OLR −49.8 W m⁻² in October; much of the western warm water carried east by anomalous surface currents.
Coupled growth with zonal advection important in the central Pacific.

Indian Ocean: cool SST along and south of the equator in the east, from strong upwelling along the equator and Sumatra; western warm anomalies from July 1997, peaking in February 1998. CPC DMI +0.55 °C (Jul) to +1.39 °C (Nov).
Reversed Walker circulation and displaced south-east trades over the Indian Ocean; Kelvin and Rossby waves; reduced latent heat loss later.

Thermocline shoaling begins in the central Pacific and propagates east; near-Date-Line westerly anomalies shift south of the equator; warm water volume falls to +0.66 and turns negative in December (−0.77 × 10¹⁴ m³).
Seasonal southward shift of the warmest water and its winds forces eastern thermocline shoaling; discharge begins.
Peak: RONI +2.28 (ONI +2.37). Eastern SST anomalies above 4 °C; December peak in the eastern and central Pacific anomaly patterns.
Mature coupled state; discharge under way.

Eastern SST stays warm despite strong subsurface cooling; off-equatorial SLP in the west turns high and easterly anomalies appear over the far western Pacific; easterlies vanish from the eastern equatorial Pacific in February 1998.
Upwelling Kelvin waves from western easterlies and boundary reflection, Rossby waves from the east, and basin discharge set up the collapse.
[61] [62] [15] [16] [14] [17]
Abrupt cooling: eastern equatorial SST falls by more than 4 °C within two weeks; about 8 °C near 0°, 130°W; cooling first centred between 125°W and 170°W. Easterlies return to the eastern Pacific.
Thermocline surfaces once the equatorial easterlies return; an MJO is implicated in the timing.
La Niña: RONI MJJ −0.46, JJA −1.05; record equatorial phytoplankton bloom.
Upwelling resumes over a discharged basin.
evidence: Warm-water recharge after the 1995–96 La Niña
WWV positive from Dec 1995 through 1996, peaking at +3.12 × 10¹⁴ m³ in Apr 1997; an ocean model attributes about 40% of the 1 June 1997 Niño 3 anomaly to the initial thermal state.
A charged reservoir lets Kelvin waves raise eastern SST and sustain growth.
A−: TAO-era observation + model decomposition for this event
A series of strong events, notably Dec 1996, Mar 1997 and Apr 1997; wind stress ≈ 50% of the 1 June Niño 3 anomaly and the main difference from 1996.
Downwelling Kelvin waves and eastward displacement of the warm-pool edge.
A: event observations + ocean-model decomposition + targeted experiments
Model SST response to the March event itself generates atmospheric responses favouring growth.
Burst-forced SST changes → more westerlies (state-dependent feedback).
A−: ocean + atmosphere GCM experiments for this event
Two exceptionally strong MJOs (Dec 1996, Feb 1997); bursts embedded in active MJO; the February MJO's Kelvin wave warms the central Pacific in late Mar–early Apr.
MJO organises bursts; rectified MJO stresses add warming; Kelvin waves advect warm water.
B: event-specific observation and budget; one intermediate-model hindcast (+50% amplitude)
Northerly cold surges from East Asia induce equatorial twin cyclones that enhance MJO bursts in late 1996 – early 1997.
B: one event-specific observational study; a second on twin cyclogenesis (title only)
Off-equatorial warm SST and cyclones accompany the switch to equatorial westerlies.
Reflection at the western boundary 'appeared favorable' before onset; minor contribution to Kelvin waves.
Reflected Rossby waves add downwelling Kelvin energy.
From May–June 1997 SOI, trades, OLR and SST strengthen together to an October–December peak.
Warming → weaker trades → deeper eastern thermocline → more warming.
B: event observations + general theory; heat budgets show zonal advection important
Bursts are more likely when the warm pool extends east, which it did through spring 1997.
Bursts partly a response to ENSO, effectively increasing coupling.
C: multi-event statistics and models, not tested for 1997 alone
Most El Niños of the past four decades preceded by spring warming and south-westerlies near the ITCZ.
Extratropical winter variability → subtropical SST → equatorial winds.
C: composite and model studies; 1997 not isolated in the abstracts read
PDO positive through 1997 (+1.6 to +2.6 in May–Jun); shallow meridional overturning at a 1992–98 low.
Weaker overturning → warmer tropical Pacific background; background alters the response to bursts.
C: decadal observations and a simple model; not event attribution
Positive IOD from mid-1997, peaking in Nov (CPC DMI +1.39 °C), after Pacific coupling.
Walker-circulation reversal → eastern upwelling; Indian Ocean coupled dynamics.
Mainly consequence; feedback on the Pacific unresolved
B: event-specific ocean model + observations; coupled-model feedback studies
TNA near or below zero in early 1997 (−0.37 °C in Mar), warm in 1998 (+0.51 °C in May).
Cool NTA in spring can favour El Niño; warming in 1998 is the usual lagged response.
C/D: index only for this event
Southward shift of westerly anomalies from Nov 1997; thermocline shoaling from the central Pacific; abrupt SST drop in May 1998.
Seasonal migration of warmest SST shifts winds south, shoaling the eastern thermocline.
A: event observations + AGCM and OGCM experiments
An MJO in May 1998 implicated in the abrupt end.
Easterly phase triggers upwelling and surfacing of the thermocline.
B: one event-specific study (abstract not available)
No large tropical eruption in 1995–97 (assessment pending a catalogue check).
RONI peak +2.28 vs ONI +2.37: the tropical-mean adjustment changes the peak by 0.09 °C.
D for event attribution; projections only
